decisions.quote: To test these predictions, we experimentally manipulated misinformation availability (high vs. low) and presented double or single misinformation. However, double versus single misinformation presentation did not affect performance or interact with misinformation availability and participants frequently reported misinformation while fully detecting discrepancies between items.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The supplied primary source file (7739d78c26609886.txt) contains only the article title ('Double misinformation and eyewitness performance: An experimental replication' by Ewa Smołka and Hartmut Blank) and abstract; the introduction, methods, results, discussion, and reference list are not present. Although the title and abstract establish an empirical replication manipulating misinformation availability (high vs. low) and double vs. single misinformation presentation, the abstract never names or cites the prior study being retested, which is why the blind target has empty citation fields. Shipped row 1547 (Blank, Panday, Edwards, Skopicz-Radkiewicz, Gibson, & Reddy, 2022, 'Double misinformation: Effects on eyewitness remembering.', DOI 10.1016/j.jarmac.2021.08.001) shares authorship and topic and is very likely the original study being replicated, but the unresolved question is that the abstract-only source text does not provide the citation needed to verify whether target_index 0 is already represented by shipped row 1547 or retests a distinct absent original. corrected_value.title: Atypical cerebral lateralisation in adults with compensated developmental dyslexia demonstrated using functional transcranial Doppler ultrasound

decisions.quote: Theories have proposed that disruption to the typical left hemisphere dominance for language may be a neurobiological correlate of language problems (e.g., Annett, 2002; Bishop, 2013; Crow et al., 1998), and empirical studies of very small samples have supported that view (Illingworth & Bishop, 2009; Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008). However, the present study did not replicate these findings, and we suggest that they are likely to have been false positives.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. (1) Empirical retesting: Wilson & Bishop (2018, PeerJ, 10.7717/peerj.4217) use functional transcranial Doppler ultrasound (fTCD) in 263 twin children (107 DLD, explicitly including 10 children meeting criteria solely on literacy/dyslexia measures on the basis of Illingworth & Bishop, 2009 [Methods, line 45], and 156 TD controls) to retest whether language/literacy disorder is associated with reduced left-hemisphere cerebral lateralisation for language (Introduction, line 4), finding no between-groups difference in fTCD laterality index (t(242.63) = 1.32, p = .190; Results, line 78) and explicitly concluding that the study failed to replicate Illingworth & Bishop (2009) (Discussion, line 106; Conclusions, line 112). (2) Source-backed identity: Confirmed in References (line 167) and Crossref metadata as Illingworth, S., & Bishop, D. (2009), 'Atypical cerebral lateralisation in adults with compensated developmental dyslexia demonstrated using functional transcranial Doppler ultrasound', Brain and Language, 111(1), 61-65, DOI 10.1016/j.bandl.2009.05.002. (3) Absence and non-equivalence: The only shipped row is input_row_index 2493 (Bishop, 2005, 'Handedness and specific language impairment: A study of 6-year-old twins', Developmental Psychobiology, DOI 10.1002/dev.20062, corresponding to sibling target_index 2), which is a behavioural handedness study in 6-year-old twins rather than an fTCD cerebral lateralisation study in dyslexic adults. Target 0 is also independent of sibling targets 1 (Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008), 3 (Hill & Bishop, 1998), and 4 (Groen et al., 2012).

corrected_value.title: A reaching test reveals weak hand preference in specific language impairment and developmental co-ordination disorder

decisions.quote: We also tested the hypothesis that children with DLD were less likely in the QHP task to reach across the midline with the right hand to a spatial position on the left side of the body, indicating weaker hand preference, as previously reported (Bishop, 2005; Hill & Bishop, 1998). A multilevel model was run with twin pair membership as a random effect, group as a between factor and spatial position as a within factor. There was a large main effect of spatial position, t(1,687.20) = 12.74, p < .001, with individuals being less likely to reach across the midline with the right hand to a spatial position on the left. However, there was no main effect of group, t(1,836.70) = 1.61, p = .108, and contrary to previous reports, no interaction between DLD status and spatial position, t(1,687.20) = 0.89, p = .376, indicating no between-groups differences in strength of hand preference.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. (1) Empirical retesting: In Methods (line 51), Results (line 90), and Discussion (line 107), the authors explicitly attempt to replicate the finding of Hill & Bishop (1998) (alongside Bishop, 2005) that children with language impairment are less likely to reach across the midline with the right hand on the Quantified Hand Preference (QHP) task, finding no main effect of group (t(1,836.70) = 1.61, p = .108) and no group-by-spatial-position interaction (t(1,687.20) = 0.89, p = .376). (2) Source-backed identity: Confirmed in References (line 165) and Crossref metadata as Hill, E., & Bishop, D. (1998), 'A reaching test reveals weak hand preference in specific language impairment and developmental co-ordination disorder', Laterality: Asymmetries of Body, Brain and Cognition, 3(4), 295-310, DOI 10.1080/713754314. (3) Absence and non-equivalence: Although both Hill & Bishop (1998) and shipped row 2493 (Bishop, 2005, 'Handedness and specific language impairment: A study of 6-year-old twins', Developmental Psychobiology, DOI 10.1002/dev.20062, sibling target_index 2) examined QHP midline reaching, they are independent primary studies on distinct samples published seven years apart (children with SLI and developmental co-ordination disorder in 1998 vs. 6-year-old twins in 2005), not alternate reports of one study. Target 3 is also distinct from sibling targets 0, 1, and 4.

decisions.quote: In the second step of analysis, we tested the relationship between language and laterality from the opposite direction, using language measures as predictors, aiming to replicate the effects reported by Groen et al. decisions.quote:
Childers and Tomasello (2001) found that training 2 1/2 -year-olds on the English transitive construction greatly improves their
                        performance on a post-test in which they must use novel verbs in that construction. In the current study, we replicated Childers
                        and Tomasello’s finding, but using a much lower frequency of transitive verbs and models in training. We also used novel verbs
                        that were of a different semantic class to our training verbs, demonstrating that semantic homogeneity is not crucial for gener-
                        alization. We also replicated the finding that 4-year-olds are significantly more productive than 2 1/2 -year-olds with the transitive
                        construction, with the new finding that this is also true for verbs of emission.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The blind coder created an unidentified target (target_index 1, with empty authors, year, title, and doi) for the statement that 4-year-olds are significantly more productive than 2.5-year-olds with the transitive construction. Full-text inspection of 7bc9ff8a5446a5aa.txt positively establishes that this age comparison is not a replication of a distinct, uncaptured primary empirical study: (1) In the Introduction (lines 48-50, left column), the authors explicitly state that 'The only transitive construction training study with pre-schoolers in which productivity was tested with novel verbs is that of Childers and Tomasello (2001)', which is already captured in shipped row input_row_index 2341 (Childers & Tomasello, 2001, 'The role of pronouns in young children's acquisition of the English transitive construction.', DOI 10.1037/0012-1649.37.6.739, matching target_index 0). (2) The general developmental benchmark that 4-year-olds are more productive with the transitive construction than 2-year-olds is attributed in the Introduction (lines 38-47, left column) to 'A number of studies' and cited solely to a review article ('see Tomasello, 2000, for a review' — Tomasello, 2000, Cognition, 74, 209-253, 'Do young children have adult syntactic competence?'), and again in the Discussion (lines 340-343, left column) to '(e.g. Tomasello, 2000)'. Under the codebook, a review article or general multi-study phenomenon is not an eligible primary original target. (3) Furthermore, the Introduction (lines 104-107, right column) states that testing 4-year-olds on novel verbs of emission was included as a novel extension ('we also checked that 4-year-olds are productive with the transitive construction with novel verbs of emission, as this had never previously been reported in the literature').
